blocks.text:
Design the core expense-sharing engine behind a Splitwise-style group expense tracker. Friends add shared expenses to a group (a paid dinner, a taxi, movie tickets) that get split among some or all of the group's members, and the system tracks every member's running net balance. The distinguishing challenge, and the single most common Splitwise interview question, is debt simplification: rather than making everyone pay back every individual expense one at a time, the system nets everyone's balances against each other and produces the smallest practical set of payments to settle the whole group up.

  • Actors: User (adds expenses, wants to settle up), SplitwiseService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: group membership, equal and exact expense splitting, per-member net balance tracking, and greedy debt simplification.

The distinguishing mechanic is debt simplification: a greedy algorithm that repeatedly matches the group's largest creditor against its largest debtor, collapsing what could be many pairwise IOUs into a minimal set of settlement transactions.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Create a group: a set of users who will share expenses together.
Add an equal-split expense: one member pays, and the amount divides evenly among a chosen set of participants.
Add an exact-split expense: one member pays, and the caller supplies exactly how much each participant owes, which must sum to the total.
Track net balances: every group member has a running balance, positive if the group owes them money, negative if they owe the group.
Simplify debts: compute the smallest practical set of settlement transactions that would bring every member's balance to zero.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting large groups with many expenses must not require touching existing split logic.
Extensibility: a new split type (percentage-based, share-based) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: split rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: simplifying debts for a group of n members runs in roughly O(n log n), dominated by repeatedly finding the current largest creditor and debtor.
Thread safety: two expenses added to the same group concurrently must never both compute balance updates from the same stale snapshot.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Is the greedy largest-creditor-versus-largest-debtor pairing acceptable, or does the interviewer want the mathematically optimal minimum number of transactions, which is a harder, NP-hard problem in general?
Can an expense be edited or deleted after it is added, and how should that affect already-computed balances?
Should percentage-based or share-based (unequal weight) splits be supported alongside equal and exact splits?
Should settlements themselves be recorded as a special kind of expense once a payment is actually made?
Is multi-currency support needed, or is a single currency assumed per group?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: The greedy largest-creditor-versus-largest-debtor pairing is used for debt simplification. It is a well-known, practical heuristic that substantially reduces the number of transactions, though it is not formally guaranteed to be the mathematically optimal minimum in every possible case.
Expense editing and deletion are out of scope; expenses are treated as immutable once added.
Only equal and exact splits are modeled; percentage and share-based splits are noted as a follow-up extension.
A single currency is assumed per group; multi-currency conversion is out of scope.
A user must already be a group member to participate in or pay for an expense in that group.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Group, User, Expense, and Settlement

items: User: a person who can belong to groups and participate in expenses.
Group: a set of members sharing expenses, tracking each member's net balance.
Expense: one shared cost, who paid it, and how it splits among participants.
Settlement: one payment from a debtor to a creditor, produced by debt simplification.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A group has many members and many expenses; every expense adjusts each affected member's net balance; simplifying a group's debts produces settlements

items: Group to User is many-to-many through membership.
Group to Expense is one-to-many.
Expense to Group balances is a side-effect relationship: adding an expense mutates the net balance of every participant plus the payer.
Group to Settlement is a derived, on-demand relationship produced only when simplifyDebts is called.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep split rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: an equal split and an exact split fundamentally disagree on how to divide an amount, evenly versus caller-supplied and validated, and that decision genuinely varies per expense.

metadata.alt: SplitStrategy interface with EqualSplitStrategy and ExactSplitStrategy implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new split type (percentage-based, share-based) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core balance-update logic in SplitwiseService. What it solves: it isolates split-calculation rules from the shared, stable balance-tracking algorithm.
Why needed: an expense being added, rejected, or a settlement being computed are all events a real expense-sharing app would want to react to (push notifications, activity feeds).

metadata.alt: ExpenseObserver interface notified by SplitwiseService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: SplitwiseService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core expense workflow from side effects.
Why needed: expense id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: ExpenseIdFactory generating sequential EXP prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every expense is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: User: attributes userId, name; responsibility: identify one person across groups.
Group: attributes groupId, name, memberIds, netBalances; responsibility: track membership and running balances for one group.
Expense: attributes expenseId, groupId, paidBy, amount, splits, description; responsibility: represent one shared cost and how it divides.
Settlement: attributes fromUserId, toUserId, amount; responsibility: represent one payment needed to net a debtor against a creditor.
SplitwiseService: the orchestrator; responsibility: validate and add expenses, maintain balances, and run debt simplification.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: SplitStrategy and ExpenseObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: SplitStrategy: computeSplits(amount, participants, exactAmounts): abstracts away exactly how an expense divides among its participants.
ExpenseObserver: onExpenseAdded / onExpenseRejected / onSettlementComputed: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover an equal-split expense, an exact-split expense, and debt simplification across the whole group.

metadata.alt: Alice pays 300 for dinner, split equally among Alice, Bob and Carol, each owing 100
Carol pays 90 for a taxi, exact split of 30 for Alice and 60 for Carol
The group's three nonzero balances collapse into two settlement transactions via greedy creditor-debtor pairing

blocks.text: The add-expense-then-simplify workflow, alongside its rejection branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Validate group membership and split totals, update balances, then optionally simplify the whole group's debts into a minimal transaction list

items: Happy path, equal split: add expense → all participants are members → equal shares computed → payer credited, each participant debited their share.
Happy path, exact split: add expense → all participants are members → exact amounts sum to the total → payer credited, each participant debited their supplied share.
Rejection paths: add expense → a participant is not a group member, or split amounts do not sum to the total, or the amount is not positive → rejected before any balance changes.
Simplification: once balances exist, repeatedly settle the current largest creditor against the current largest debtor until every balance reaches zero.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: addExpense(groupId, paidBy, amount, participants, strategy, exactAmounts): validates and applies one shared expense to the group's balances.
simplifyDebts(groupId): returns the minimal-effort list of settlement transactions to zero out every member's balance.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InvalidSplitException: exact split amounts do not sum to the expense total.
UserNotInGroupException: a participant or payer is not a member of the group.
InvalidExpenseException: a non-positive expense amount was supplied.

blocks.text: The critical race is two expenses added to the same group at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to update the same group's balances; synchronization ensures one expense's updates commit before the other reads the current balances

blocks.text: Synchronizing the balance-update step per group ensures two concurrent expenses can never both compute their updates from the same stale balance snapshot, which would otherwise silently drop one expense's effect.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new split type (percentage-based, share-weighted) is a new SplitStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (push notification, activity feed entry) is a new ExpenseObserver implementation.
Recording an actual settlement payment can be added as a new expense-like record that reduces both parties' balances without going through the split logic.
Multi-currency support can be layered on by attaching a currency to each group and converting at the point balances are compared.
Single Responsibility: Group tracks membership and balances, SplitStrategy decides split rules, ExpenseObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new split types or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to SplitwiseService.
Liskov Substitution: any SplitStrategy or ExpenseObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: ExpenseObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: SplitwiseService depends on the SplitStrategy and ExpenseObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.

An expense where the payer is also a participant only nets the payer's own share against what they paid, rather than crediting the full amount and separately debiting their share as two unrelated numbers.
A group where every member's balance is already zero produces an empty settlement list from simplifyDebts, not an error.
An exact split whose amounts sum to the total within floating point tolerance (not requiring bit-for-bit equality) is accepted, since real currency amounts often involve rounding.
A participant appearing twice in the same expense's participant list is treated as a single share, not double-counted.
addExpense: O(k) where k is the number of participants in the expense.
simplifyDebts: O(n log n) for n group members, dominated by repeatedly extracting the current largest creditor and debtor.
Space: O(users + groups + expenses) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: User, Group, GroupMember, Expense, and ExpenseSplit

items: GroupMember stores the running netBalance per user per group, avoiding a full replay of every expense on each balance read.
ExpenseSplit is a separate table since one expense can have many participant shares, a genuine one-to-many relationship.
Support percentage-based and share-weighted splits as additional SplitStrategy implementations.
Record actual settlement payments once made, so simplifyDebts reflects real-world partial progress.
Support expense editing and deletion with correct balance reversal.
Explore a more computationally expensive but provably optimal minimum-transaction algorithm for very small, high-value groups where minimizing transaction count matters more than raw performance.

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class InvalidSplitException(Exception): pass
class UserNotInGroupException(Exception): pass
class InvalidExpenseException(Exception): pass

# The core expense-sharing engine tying every piece together.
class SplitwiseService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.groups = {}       # groupId -> Group
        self.users = {}          # userId -> User
        self.observers = []         # listeners

    def add_user(self, user):
        self.users[user.user_id] = user  # register a user

    def add_group(self, group):
        self.groups[group.group_id] = group  # register a group

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def add_expense(self, group_id, paid_by, amount, participants, strategy, exact_amounts, factory):
        group = self.groups[group_id]  # the group this expense belongs to
        if amount <= 0:  # reject non-positive amounts
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_expense_rejected(group_id, "Invalid amount")
            raise InvalidExpenseException("Amount must be positive")
        if not group.is_member(paid_by):  # payer must be a member
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_expense_rejected(group_id, "Payer not in group")
            raise UserNotInGroupException(f"Payer {paid_by} is not in group {group_id}")
        for participant in participants:  # every participant must be a member
            if not group.is_member(participant):
                for obs in self.observers:
                    obs.on_expense_rejected(group_id, "Participant not in group")
                raise UserNotInGroupException(f"Participant {participant} is not in group {group_id}")
        splits = strategy.compute_splits(amount, participants, exact_amounts)  # may raise InvalidSplitException
        expense_id = factory.next_expense_id()  # build id
        group.adjust_balance(paid_by, amount)  # payer is credited the full amount
        for user_id, share in splits.items():  # each participant is debited their share
            group.adjust_balance(user_id, -share)
        expense = Expense(expense_id, group_id, paid_by, amount, splits, "expense")  # build the record
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_expense_added(expense)  # notify
        return expense  # hand back the recorded expense

    def simplify_debts(self, group_id):
        group = self.groups[group_id]  # the group to settle up
        balances = {member_id: group.get_balance(member_id) for member_id in group.member_ids}  # snapshot balances
        settlements = []  # accumulated result

        while True:
            max_creditor = None  # member with the largest positive balance
            max_debtor = None      # member with the largest negative balance
            for user_id, balance in balances.items():
                if max_creditor is None or balance > balances[max_creditor]:
                    max_creditor = user_id  # track the largest creditor
                if max_debtor is None or balance < balances[max_debtor]:
                    max_debtor = user_id  # track the largest debtor
            credit_amount = balances[max_creditor]  # how much the creditor is owed
            debt_amount = -balances[max_debtor]  # how much the debtor owes
            if credit_amount < 0.001 or debt_amount < 0.001:
                break  # everyone is settled up
            settle_amount = min(credit_amount, debt_amount)  # settle the smaller of the two
            settlements.append(Settlement(max_debtor, max_creditor, settle_amount))  # record this payment
            balances[max_creditor] = credit_amount-settle_amount  # reduce the creditor's remaining balance
            balances[max_debtor] = -(debt_amount-settle_amount)  # reduce the debtor's remaining balance

        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_settlement_computed(settlements)  # notify
        return settlements  # the minimal-effort list of payments

items: Why greedily pair the largest creditor against the largest debtor rather than settling expenses pairwise as they happen? Because settling every individual expense pairwise can require far more transactions than necessary; netting balances first and then simplifying produces noticeably fewer real-world payments, which is the entire point of the feature.

Is the greedy algorithm guaranteed to produce the mathematically minimum number of transactions? Not in every case, that general problem is NP-hard, but the greedy largest-versus-largest pairing is simple, fast, and empirically very close to optimal, which is why it is the standard answer in interviews and in Splitwise itself.

How would you extend this to record when a settlement is actually paid? Add a recordSettlement method that behaves like a two-person expense, adjusting both parties' balances directly without going through a SplitStrategy at all.

Greedy simplification vs an exact minimum-transaction solver: greedy runs in O(n log n) and is simple to implement and reason about, at the cost of not being provably optimal; an exact solver could find fewer transactions in rare cases but is far more complex and slower, overkill for most group sizes.

Running net balance per member vs replaying every expense on read: a running balance gives O(1) reads at the cost of needing careful synchronization on writes; replaying every expense would always be correct by construction but scale poorly as a group's expense history grows.

Immutable expenses vs editable expenses: immutability keeps balance bookkeeping simple and auditable, at the cost of needing a correcting entry rather than a true edit when someone makes a mistake entering an expense.
Persist users, groups, expenses, and per-member balances in a relational database using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit expense and settlement events to a message queue so downstream systems (push notifications, activity feeds) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Cache each group's current balances in memory or a fast key-value store, invalidated on every new expense, to keep simplifyDebts fast for large, active groups.
Add audit logging around every balance mutation, since money-adjacent bugs are far more costly to leave silently unnoticed than in most other domains.
